\begin{abstract}
We develop, from first principles and in complete detail, the theory of \emph{empirical
Rademacher complexity} as a measure of the capacity of a hypothesis class, and use it to
establish generalization bounds for supervised learning. Working with the exact finite
average over the $2^n$ sign patterns of a sample of size $n$, we establish: (i) the basic
calculus of the complexity functional --- vanishing on singletons, monotonicity,
nonnegativity, and boundedness by any uniform bound on the outputs; (ii) the \emph{margin
bound} $\Rad \le WB/\sqrt{n}$ for linear predictors of weight-norm at most $W$ on sample
points of norm at most $B$ in an \emph{arbitrary} real inner product space, together with its
kernel form, which depends on the kernel only through $\sup_x K(x,x)$; (iii) \emph{Massart's
finite class lemma} $\Rad \le r\sqrt{2\log N}/n$ together with the exact evaluation
$\Rad(\{-1,1\}^n) = 1$, showing the lemma tight up to the single absolute constant
$\sqrt{2\log 2}\in[1,6/5)$; (iv) the exact evaluation $\Rad(\Ball_n(r)) = r/\sqrt{n}$ for the
Euclidean ball, the fact that this class is infinite --- so every counting-based bound is
vacuous for it --- and the quantitative statement that any dimension-dependent bound
$c\sqrt{d/n}$ is strictly worse than the margin bound once $d > (WB/c)^2$; and (v) the
\emph{symmetrization inequality}
$\E_S[\sup_f(\E f - \Ehat_S f)] \le 2\,\E_S[\Rad_S(\Fclass)]$ over a finite domain with an
arbitrary product measure, from which we deduce the generalization bound
$2B\sqrt{2\log N/n}$ for finite classes. Together these give a sharp two-regime picture: on
unstructured finite classes counting is essentially optimal, while on geometrically
constrained continuous classes counting is infinitely loose and the Rademacher measurement is
exact.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} Rademacher complexity, generalization bound, margin bound, kernel
methods, symmetrization, Massart's lemma, VC dimension, statistical learning theory.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The problem}

A learning algorithm sees a finite sample and returns a hypothesis that performs well on it.
The central question of statistical learning theory is: when does good performance on the
sample imply good performance on the underlying distribution? Since the algorithm selects the
hypothesis \emph{after} seeing the data, the guarantee must be uniform over the hypothesis
class $\Fclass$; the quantity to control is
\[
  \gap(S) \;=\; \sup_{f\in\Fclass}\bigl(\E f - \Ehat_S f\bigr),
\]
where $\Ehat_S f = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)$ is the empirical mean on the sample
$S = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and $\E f$ the true mean.

The classical answer measures $\Fclass$ combinatorially, via the \emph{VC dimension} --- the
largest $n$ for which $\Fclass$ realizes all $2^n$ labelings of some $n$ points --- and yields
bounds of the shape $c\sqrt{d/n}$. This has two defects. First, it is distribution-free to a
fault. Second, and more seriously, it is a \emph{counting} bound: it degenerates when the class
realizes infinitely many behaviours on the sample, which is the generic situation for
real-valued predictors and for every kernel method.

\subsection{Contribution}

We build the alternative --- Rademacher complexity --- from the ground up, with all statements
precise and all constants explicit. Three features distinguish the development.

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Exact values, not just bounds.} We compute $\Rad$ exactly for two fundamental
classes: the full sign cube (value $1$) and the Euclidean ball of radius $r$ (value
$r/\sqrt n$). Exact values make the comparison with counting bounds decisive rather than
suggestive.
\item \textbf{Complete dimension-freedom.} The margin bound is proved in an arbitrary real
inner product space, with no finiteness or separability hypothesis. This licenses the kernel
form.
\item \textbf{A quantitative separation.} We prove a precise threshold beyond which any
dimension-dependent bound is strictly weaker than the dimension-free margin bound, and exhibit
a class on which counting bounds are not merely weak but vacuous.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Definitions and the Basic Calculus}

Throughout, $n\ge 1$ is the sample size.

\begin{definition}[Sign patterns]
A \emph{sign pattern} is a vector $\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}^n$. There are $2^n$ of them and the
\emph{Rademacher distribution} is the uniform distribution on this set. Two identities are used
constantly: $\lvert\sigma_i\rvert = 1$ and $\sigma_i^2 = 1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Sign average]
For a sign pattern $\sigma$ and $v\in\R^n$, the \emph{sign average} is
$A_\sigma(v) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i v_i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Empirical Rademacher complexity]
For $F\subseteq\R^n$,
\[
  \Rad(F) \;=\; \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n}\ \sup_{v\in F} A_\sigma(v).
\]
If $\Fclass$ is a class of functions $X\to\R$ and $S = (x_1,\dots,x_n)$ a sample, we write
$\Rad_S(\Fclass) = \Rad(F_S)$ where $F_S = \{(f(x_1),\dots,f(x_n)) : f\in\Fclass\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Interpretation]
$A_\sigma(v)$ is the empirical correlation of the outputs $v$ with the random $\pm1$ labels
$\sigma$. Thus $\Rad(F)$ measures, on average over label noise, how well the \emph{best} member
of the class fits pure noise.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Sign-flip symmetry]\label{lem:flip}
The map $\sigma\mapsto-\sigma$ is an involution of the set of sign patterns; hence
$\sum_\sigma g(-\sigma) = \sum_\sigma g(\sigma)$ for every $g$. In particular
$\sum_\sigma \sigma_i = 0$ for every coordinate $i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Negation is a self-inverse bijection of the index set, so it merely reindexes the sum. Taking
$g(\sigma)=\sigma_i$ gives $\sum_\sigma\sigma_i = -\sum_\sigma\sigma_i$, whence the sum is zero.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Decorrelation]\label{lem:decorr}
For $i\ne j$, $\sum_\sigma \sigma_i\sigma_j = 0$; and $\sum_\sigma\sigma_i^2 = 2^n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Flipping only the $i$-th coordinate is an involution of the sign patterns which negates
$\sigma_i$ and fixes $\sigma_j$, hence negates the summand; reindexing shows the sum equals its
own negative. The second claim follows from $\sigma_i^2=1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Singletons have zero complexity]\label{thm:singleton}
For any $v\in\R^n$, $\Rad(\{v\}) = 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The supremum over a singleton is $A_\sigma(v)$, so
$\Rad(\{v\}) = 2^{-n}\sum_\sigma\frac1n\sum_i\sigma_i v_i$. Exchanging summation order,
each inner sum is $v_i\sum_\sigma\sigma_i = 0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:flip}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity]
If $F\subseteq G$, $F\ne\emptyset$, and each $\sup_{v\in G}A_\sigma(v)$ is finite, then
$\Rad(F)\le\Rad(G)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For each $\sigma$ the image sets are nested, so the suprema are ordered; sum and divide by
$2^n>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity]
If $F\ne\emptyset$ and all suprema are finite, then $\Rad(F)\ge 0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $v\in F$. For each $\sigma$, $\sup_u A_\sigma(u)\ge A_\sigma(v)$ and
$\sup_u A_{-\sigma}(u)\ge A_{-\sigma}(v) = -A_\sigma(v)$; the pair contributes a nonnegative
total. Summing over $\sigma$ and using Lemma~\ref{lem:flip} to identify
$\sum_\sigma\sup_u A_{-\sigma}(u)$ with $\sum_\sigma\sup_u A_\sigma(u)$ gives
$2\sum_\sigma\sup_u A_\sigma(u)\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Uniform output bound]
Let $B\ge0$. If $\lvert v_i\rvert\le B$ for all $v\in F$ and all $i$, then $\Rad(F)\le B$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$A_\sigma(v)\le\frac1n\sum_i\lvert\sigma_i\rvert\,\lvert v_i\rvert\le B$ for each $\sigma$ and
$v$; average.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Sandwich principle]\label{lem:sandwich}
If $\sup_{v\in F}A_\sigma(v)\le c$ for every $\sigma$ then $\Rad(F)\le c$; if
$\sup_{v\in F}A_\sigma(v)\ge c$ for every $\sigma$ then $\Rad(F)\ge c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Average the pointwise inequality over the $2^n$ patterns.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:sandwich} is the workhorse for exact computations: if the supremum takes the
\emph{same} value for every sign pattern --- as happens for both the cube and the ball, by
symmetry --- that value \emph{is} the complexity.

\section{Symmetrization}

We work over a finite domain $X$ with a probability vector $p:X\to[0,\infty)$,
$\sum_x p(x)=1$, and the product measure on samples, $w(S)=\prod_{i=1}^n p(S_i)$ for $S\in X^n$.
All expectations are explicit finite sums.

\begin{definition}
For a finite nonempty class $\Fclass$ of functions $X\to\R$: the empirical mean
$\Ehat_S f = \frac1n\sum_i f(S_i)$ and true mean $\E f = \sum_x p(x)f(x)$; the signed empirical
average $C_\sigma(S,f) = \frac1n\sum_i\sigma_i f(S_i)$; the empirical Rademacher complexity
$\Rad_S(\Fclass) = 2^{-n}\sum_\sigma\max_{f}C_\sigma(S,f)$; and the uniform deviation
$\gap(S) = \max_f(\E f - \Ehat_S f)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Product measure basics]\label{lem:prod}
$w(S)\ge0$; $\sum_S w(S) = 1$; the $i$-th marginal is $p$, i.e.
$\sum_S w(S)g(S_i) = \sum_x p(x)g(x)$. Consequently $\sum_S w(S)\Ehat_S f = \E f$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The total mass factorizes as $\prod_i(\sum_x p(x)) = 1$. For the marginal, sum out the $n-1$
coordinates $j\ne i$, each contributing a factor $1$. Unbiasedness follows by linearity.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetrization]\label{thm:sym}
For a finite nonempty class $\Fclass$ and $n\ge1$,
\[
  \sum_S w(S)\,\gap(S) \;\le\; 2\sum_S w(S)\,\Rad_S(\Fclass),
  \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad
  \E_S[\gap(S)] \le 2\,\E_S[\Rad_S(\Fclass)].
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1 (ghost sample).} Introduce an independent copy $S'$ with the same product law and
set $G(S,S') = \max_f\frac1n\sum_i(f(S'_i)-f(S_i))$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:prod},
$\E f = \sum_{S'}w(S')\Ehat_{S'}f$ for each fixed $f$, so
\[
  \gap(S) = \max_f\sum_{S'}w(S')\bigl(\Ehat_{S'}f - \Ehat_S f\bigr)
  \le \sum_{S'}w(S')\,G(S,S'),
\]
since the maximum of a weighted average is at most the weighted average of the maxima. Weighting
by $w(S)$ and summing gives
$\sum_S w(S)\gap(S)\le\sum_{S,S'}w(S)w(S')G(S,S')$.

\emph{Step 2 (swap invariance).} For a sign pattern $\sigma$ let $T_\sigma$ exchange
$S_i\leftrightarrow S'_i$ for every $i$ with $\sigma_i=-1$. Then $T_\sigma$ is an involution of
$X^n\times X^n$ preserving the product weight $w(S)w(S')$, since it permutes the factors; and
$G(T_\sigma(S,S')) = \max_f\frac1n\sum_i\sigma_i(f(S'_i)-f(S_i))$, because exchanging the $i$-th
pair negates the $i$-th difference. Reindexing therefore gives, for \emph{every} $\sigma$,
\[
  \sum_{S,S'}w(S)w(S')G(S,S')
  = \sum_{S,S'}w(S)w(S')\max_f\frac1n\sum_i\sigma_i\bigl(f(S'_i)-f(S_i)\bigr).
\]

\emph{Step 3 (split).} Average over the $2^n$ sign patterns and use
$\max_f(a_f+b_f)\le\max_f a_f+\max_f b_f$ to split the maximum into
$\max_f C_\sigma(S',f) + \max_f(-C_\sigma(S,f))$. Averaging the second term over $\sigma$ and
applying Lemma~\ref{lem:flip} turns it into $\max_f C_\sigma(S,f)$. Since $S$ and $S'$ have the
same law, the total is $2\sum_S w(S)\Rad_S(\Fclass)$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:sym} is why the noise-fitting measurement is meaningful: \emph{the expected
uniform overfitting of a class is at most twice its expected ability to fit random labels.}

\section{Counting: Massart's Lemma and Its Exact Tightness}

\begin{theorem}[Massart's finite class lemma]\label{thm:massart}
Let $F\subseteq\R^n$ be finite and nonempty with $N=\lvert F\rvert$ and
$\sum_i v_i^2\le r^2$ for every $v\in F$, where $r\ge0$. Then
\[
  \Rad(F) \;\le\; \frac{r\sqrt{2\log N}}{n}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $N=1$ both sides vanish by Theorem~\ref{thm:singleton}; assume $N\ge2$, so $L:=\log N>0$. If
$r=0$ then $F=\{0\}$ and both sides vanish; assume $r>0$. Put
$M(\sigma) = \max_{v\in F}\sum_i\sigma_i v_i$, so $\Rad(F) = \frac1n 2^{-n}\sum_\sigma M(\sigma)$.

Fix $\lambda>0$. Jensen's inequality for $t\mapsto e^t$ under the uniform measure on sign
patterns gives $\exp(\lambda\,2^{-n}\sum_\sigma M(\sigma))\le 2^{-n}\sum_\sigma e^{\lambda M(\sigma)}$.
Bounding the exponentiated maximum by a sum over the class,
\[
  2^{-n}\sum_\sigma e^{\lambda M(\sigma)}
  \le \sum_{v\in F} 2^{-n}\sum_\sigma\exp\Bigl(\lambda\sum_i\sigma_i v_i\Bigr).
\]
The inner average is the Rademacher moment generating function and factorizes exactly:
\[
  2^{-n}\sum_\sigma\exp\Bigl(\lambda\sum_i\sigma_i v_i\Bigr)
  = \prod_{i=1}^n\frac{e^{\lambda v_i}+e^{-\lambda v_i}}{2}
  = \prod_{i=1}^n\cosh(\lambda v_i).
\]
The elementary inequality $\cosh t\le e^{t^2/2}$ (compare Taylor coefficients:
$1/(2k)!\le1/(2^k k!)$) gives $\prod_i\cosh(\lambda v_i)\le\exp(\lambda^2 r^2/2)$. Taking
logarithms yields $2^{-n}\sum_\sigma M(\sigma)\le L/\lambda + \lambda r^2/2$; choosing
$\lambda=\sqrt{2L}/r$, which balances the two terms, gives $r\sqrt{2L}$. Divide by $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Sign cube]
$Q_n = \{-1,+1\}^n\subseteq\R^n$: the restriction to the sample of a class that shatters it.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Exact complexity of the cube]\label{thm:cube}
For $n\ge1$, $\Rad(Q_n) = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix $\sigma$. For any $v\in Q_n$, $\sum_i\sigma_i v_i\le n$, since each product of signs is at
most $1$; and $v=\sigma\in Q_n$ attains $\sum_i\sigma_i^2 = n$. So
$\max_{v\in Q_n}A_\sigma(v)=1$ for every $\sigma$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sandwich}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tightness of Massart's lemma]\label{thm:tight}
For $n\ge1$: the exact complexity of $Q_n$ is $1$; Massart's bound applied to $Q_n$, where
$N=2^n$ and $r=\sqrt n$, evaluates to
\[
  \frac{\sqrt n\,\sqrt{2\log 2^n}}{n} \;=\; \sqrt{2\log 2},
\]
independently of $n$; and $1\le\sqrt{2\log2}<\tfrac65$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Use $\log 2^n = n\log 2$ and $\sqrt{2n\log2} = \sqrt n\sqrt{2\log2}$, so the expression is
$\sqrt n\sqrt n\sqrt{2\log2}/n$. The numerical bracket follows from $\log 2 > 1/2$ and
$\log 2 < 18/25$, whence $2\log 2 < 36/25 = (6/5)^2$.
\end{proof}

On the hardest possible class Massart's counting bound overestimates the truth by the fixed
factor $\sqrt{2\log2}\approx1.1774$ --- under $18\%$ --- for every sample size. The
$\sqrt{\log N}$ shape is therefore the correct behaviour for unstructured finite classes, not an
artifact of a lossy proof.

\begin{corollary}[Generalization for finite classes]\label{cor:fingen}
Let $\Fclass$ be a finite nonempty class of $N$ functions on a finite domain with
$\lvert f(x)\rvert\le B$ for all $f,x$. Then for every sample of size $n\ge1$,
\[
  \Rad_S(\Fclass) \;\le\; \frac{B\sqrt{2\log N}}{\sqrt n},
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \E_S\Bigl[\sup_{f}\bigl(\E f - \Ehat_S f\bigr)\Bigr] \;\le\; 2B\sqrt{\frac{2\log N}{n}}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The behaviour vectors satisfy $\sum_i f(S_i)^2\le nB^2$, i.e.\ length $\le B\sqrt n$;
Theorem~\ref{thm:massart} with $r=B\sqrt n$ gives $B\sqrt{2\log N}/\sqrt n$. Averaging this
uniform-in-$S$ bound against the product weights (total mass $1$) and inserting it into
Theorem~\ref{thm:sym} gives the second display.
\end{proof}

\section{Geometry: The Euclidean Ball and the Collapse of Counting}

\begin{definition}
For $r\ge0$, $\Ball_n(r) = \{v\in\R^n : \sum_{i=1}^n v_i^2\le r^2\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Cauchy--Schwarz]\label{lem:ballub}
For $r\ge0$, $n\ge1$, $v\in\Ball_n(r)$ and any $\sigma$: $A_\sigma(v)\le r/\sqrt n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\sum_i\sigma_i v_i\le(\sum_i\sigma_i^2)^{1/2}(\sum_i v_i^2)^{1/2}\le\sqrt n\,r$; divide by $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Attainment]\label{lem:ballatt}
For $n\ge1$ and any $\sigma$, the vector $v^\sigma = \frac{r}{\sqrt n}\sigma$ lies in
$\Ball_n(r)$ and satisfies $A_\sigma(v^\sigma) = r/\sqrt n$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\sum_i(v_i^\sigma)^2 = \frac{r^2}{n}\sum_i\sigma_i^2 = r^2$, and
$A_\sigma(v^\sigma) = \frac1n\cdot n\cdot\frac{r}{\sqrt n} = \frac{r}{\sqrt n}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact complexity of the ball]\label{thm:ball}
For $r\ge0$ and $n\ge1$, $\;\Rad(\Ball_n(r)) = r/\sqrt n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemmas~\ref{lem:ballub} and \ref{lem:ballatt} the supremum is attained and equals
$r/\sqrt n$ for every $\sigma$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sandwich} in both directions.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dimension-free bound for subclasses]\label{thm:subball}
If $F\subseteq\Ball_n(r)$ then $\Rad(F)\le r/\sqrt n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Lemma~\ref{lem:ballub} and Lemma~\ref{lem:sandwich}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The ball is infinite]\label{thm:ballinf}
For $r>0$ and $n\ge1$, $\Ball_n(r)$ is an infinite set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The map $t\mapsto(t,0,\dots,0)$ is injective on $[0,r]$ and lands in $\Ball_n(r)$, since
$t^2\le r^2$ there; an injective image of an infinite set is infinite.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Failure of counting]\label{cor:fail}
Every bound on $\Rad$ obtained by counting the number $N$ of behaviours of the class on the
sample --- Massart's lemma, growth-function bounds, Sauer--Shelah bounds, and hence the
standard VC route --- is vacuous for $\Ball_n(r)$ with $r>0$: it asserts only $\Rad\le\infty$.
Yet the true value is the finite, exactly known number $r/\sqrt n$.
\end{corollary}

Counting is not merely ``loose'' for the ball; it is silent. The Rademacher functional sees the
correct geometric fact: the ball is small in the Euclidean metric even though it is uncountable
as a set, and Euclidean smallness is what noise-fitting responds to.

\section{The Margin Bound for Linear and Kernel Classes}

Let $E$ be a real inner product space, with \emph{no assumption on its dimension}.

\begin{definition}[Linear class on a sample]
For $W\ge0$ and $x_1,\dots,x_n\in E$,
\[
  \mathcal{L}_W(x) = \bigl\{v\in\R^n : \exists\,w\in E,\ \norm{w}\le W,\ v_i = \ip{w}{x_i}\ \forall i\bigr\}.
\]
This class is nonempty (take $w=0$).
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Cauchy--Schwarz in feature space]\label{lem:cs}
For every sign pattern $\sigma$,
$\displaystyle \sup_{v\in\mathcal{L}_W(x)}A_\sigma(v)\le\frac{W}{n}\Bigl\lVert\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i x_i\Bigr\rVert$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $v$ generated by $w$ with $\norm{w}\le W$, linearity gives
$\sum_i\sigma_i\ip{w}{x_i} = \bigl\langle w,\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\bigr\rangle
\le\norm{w}\bigl\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\bigr\rVert\le W\bigl\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\bigr\rVert$.
Divide by $n$ and take the supremum.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Second moment of the signed sum]\label{lem:secmom}
For any $x_1,\dots,x_n\in E$,
\[
  \sum_\sigma\Bigl\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\Bigr\rVert^2 = 2^n\sum_{i=1}^n\norm{x_i}^2,
  \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad
  \E_\sigma\Bigl\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\Bigr\rVert^2 = \sum_i\norm{x_i}^2.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Expanding bilinearly, $\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\rVert^2 = \sum_i\sum_j\sigma_i\sigma_j\ip{x_i}{x_j}$.
Sum over $\sigma$ and exchange the order of summation. By Lemma~\ref{lem:decorr} the
off-diagonal terms vanish and each diagonal term contributes $2^n\norm{x_i}^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Margin bound for linear predictors]\label{thm:margin}
Let $W,B\ge0$, $n\ge1$, and let $x_1,\dots,x_n\in E$ satisfy $\norm{x_i}\le B$ for all $i$. Then
\[
  \Rad\bigl(\mathcal{L}_W(x)\bigr) \;\le\; \frac{WB}{\sqrt n}.
\]
No hypothesis is made on $\dim E$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $u(\sigma) = \lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\rVert$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cs},
$\sum_\sigma\sup_v A_\sigma(v)\le\frac{W}{n}\sum_\sigma u(\sigma)$. By Cauchy--Schwarz over the
$2^n$ sign patterns, $(\sum_\sigma u(\sigma))^2\le2^n\sum_\sigma u(\sigma)^2$, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:secmom} with $\norm{x_i}\le B$,
$\sum_\sigma u(\sigma)^2 = 2^n\sum_i\norm{x_i}^2\le 2^n nB^2$. Hence
$(\sum_\sigma u(\sigma))^2\le(2^n\sqrt n B)^2$, and since $u\ge0$,
$\sum_\sigma u(\sigma)\le2^n\sqrt nB$. Therefore
$\Rad(\mathcal{L}_W(x))\le 2^{-n}\cdot\frac{W}{n}\cdot2^n\sqrt nB = WB/\sqrt n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Where the $\sqrt n$ comes from]
Passing through Theorem~\ref{thm:subball} instead would be weaker: the behaviour vectors of
$\mathcal{L}_W(x)$ have Euclidean length at most $WB\sqrt n$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:subball} yields
only $\Rad\le WB$. The extra factor $1/\sqrt n$ is purchased entirely by \emph{cancellation}:
the identity $\E_\sigma[\sigma_i\sigma_j]=0$ replaces the worst-case bound
$\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\rVert\le nB$ by the root-mean-square bound $\sqrt nB$. Linear classes
are learnable not just because they are bounded, but because signed sums of data vectors cancel.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Kernel margin bound]\label{thm:kernel}
Let $X$ be any set, $\varphi:X\to E$ a feature map, and $K(y,z) = \ip{\varphi(y)}{\varphi(z)}$ the
associated kernel. Let $W,B\ge0$ and let $s_1,\dots,s_n\in X$ satisfy $K(s_i,s_i)\le B^2$. Then
the class of kernel predictors $y\mapsto\ip{w}{\varphi(y)}$ with $\norm{w}\le W$, restricted to
the sample, has $\Rad\le WB/\sqrt n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\norm{\varphi(s_i)}^2 = K(s_i,s_i)\le B^2$, so $\norm{\varphi(s_i)}\le B$; apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:margin} to the sample $\varphi(s_1),\dots,\varphi(s_n)$ in $E$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Only the diagonal matters]
The bound depends on the kernel solely through $\sup_i K(s_i,s_i)$. Off-diagonal structure, the
dimension of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and even its separability are irrelevant.
\end{remark}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
Kernel & $K(x,x)$ & Feature dimension & Complexity bound\\
\midrule
Linear, $\norm{x}\le B$ & $\le B^2$ & $d$ & $WB/\sqrt n$\\
Polynomial $(1+\ip{x}{y})^q$, $\norm{x}\le1$ & $\le 2^q$ & $\binom{d+q}{q}$ & $W2^{q/2}/\sqrt n$\\

\end{tabular}
\caption{The Gaussian row is the point of the theory: an infinite-dimensional hypothesis class
with a finite, small, explicitly computed complexity bound.}
\end{table}

\begin{theorem}[Dimension dependence is eventually fatal]\label{thm:vcworse}
Let $W,B,c>0$ and $n\ge1$. If $d > (WB/c)^2$, then
\[
  \frac{WB}{\sqrt n} \;<\; c\sqrt{\frac{d}{n}}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $\sqrt{d/n} = \sqrt d/\sqrt n$ and $\sqrt{\cdot}$ is strictly increasing, $d>(WB/c)^2$
gives $\sqrt d>WB/c$, i.e.\ $c\sqrt d>WB$; divide by $\sqrt n>0$.
\end{proof}

Linear predictors through the origin in $\R^d$ have VC dimension $d$ (with a bias term, $d+1$),
so any bound derived from that combinatorial parameter has the shape $c\sqrt{d/n}$. Whatever the
constant $c$, there is a finite threshold $d_0 = (WB/c)^2$ beyond which the dimension-free
margin bound is strictly better, and the ratio of the two bounds grows like $\sqrt d$. Combining
with Corollary~\ref{cor:fail}, the comparison has two independent teeth: qualitatively, counting
bounds are vacuous for continuous classes such as $\Ball_n(r)$ while the Rademacher value is
exact; quantitatively, even a finite dimension-dependent bound is strictly worse once
$d>(WB/c)^2$.

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Exact complexity of a finite class.}
For $F=\{v^{(1)},\dots,v^{(N)}\}\subseteq\R^n$ the definition is a finite average, so it can be
evaluated exactly by enumerating all $2^n$ sign patterns, at cost $\Theta(2^nNn)$ time and
$\Theta(Nn)$ space. This is feasible for $n\lesssim20$ and is what one needs to verify the
theoretical bounds on small examples.

\paragraph{Monte Carlo estimation.}
For larger $n$, sample $m$ sign patterns uniformly and average. The estimator is unbiased with
variance $O(1/m)$; under a uniform output bound $B$, Hoeffding's inequality gives additive error
$O(B\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/m})$ with probability $1-\delta$. Cost $\Theta(mNn)$, or
$\Theta(m\cdot\mathrm{fit}(n))$ when the inner maximum is realized by running the learning
algorithm on random labels. This last variant is the practically important one: the complexity of
a class as implemented by an actual optimizer can be estimated by training on random labels.

\paragraph{Closed forms for structured classes.}
For the ball, the supremum equals $r/\sqrt n$ for every $\sigma$, so the answer is available in
$O(1)$ time. For the linear class the supremum for a given $\sigma$ equals
$\frac{W}{n}\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\rVert$ exactly (the maximizer is $W$ times the unit vector in
the direction of the signed sum), so
$\Rad = \frac{W}{n}\E_\sigma\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i x_i\rVert$ exactly; bounding
$\E_\sigma\lVert\cdot\rVert\le(\E_\sigma\lVert\cdot\rVert^2)^{1/2}\le\sqrt nB$ recovers
Theorem~\ref{thm:margin}. In the kernel case the same quantity is computable from the Gram matrix
alone, since $\lVert\sum_i\sigma_i\varphi(s_i)\rVert^2 = \sigma^\top G\sigma$, at cost
$\Theta(mn^2)$ after an $\Theta(n^2)$ Gram computation; the feature map is never needed.

\paragraph{Bound selection.}
Given a class one may hold several bounds at once and should report the minimum,
\[
  \Rad \le \min\Bigl\{B,\ \tfrac{r\sqrt{2\log N}}{n}\ (N<\infty),\
  \tfrac{r}{\sqrt n}\ (F\subseteq\Ball_n(r)),\ \tfrac{WB}{\sqrt n}\ (\text{linear/kernel})\Bigr\}.
\]

\section{Applications}

\paragraph{Support vector machines and kernel methods.}
A soft-margin SVM with regularization constrains $\norm{w}\le W$, and the data enter only through
$\sup_x K(x,x)$. Theorem~\ref{thm:kernel} gives $\Rad\le WB/\sqrt n$ and Theorem~\ref{thm:sym}
converts this into a generalization guarantee. For a normalized kernel the guarantee is
$W/\sqrt n$, independent of everything else about the kernel: the precise sense in which the
kernel trick is free.

\paragraph{Regularization as capacity control.}
Theorem~\ref{thm:margin} says capacity is $WB/\sqrt n$, linear in the weight-norm budget. Weight
decay, $\ell_2$ regularization, margin maximization, and constrained optimization all reduce $W$;
the theory identifies $W$ as the exact quantity being paid for.

\paragraph{The overparameterization paradox.}
Modern models have far more parameters than training examples, so every dimension-dependent bound
is vacuous. Theorem~\ref{thm:vcworse} shows this is evidence against the parameter count as a
capacity measure, not against learning theory: the margin bound is uniformly better for
$d>(WB/c)^2$ and remains finite as $d\to\infty$.

\paragraph{Random-label diagnostics.}
The definition of $\Rad$ is operationally ``train on random labels and measure the fit''. A model
achieving near-perfect accuracy on random labels has $\Rad$ near its output scale, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:sym} then offers no nontrivial guarantee --- correctly, since such a class can be
fooled by a finite sample. The diagnostic is not a heuristic proxy for the theory; it is the
theory.

\section{Discussion, Limitations, and Future Work}

\subsection{Limitations}
The bounds are in expectation over the sample; high-probability statements require a
concentration step. The symmetrization argument is carried out over a finite domain with explicit
product weights so that all expectations are finite sums; extending to general probability spaces
requires measurability side conditions on the supremum. The margin bound applies to the scores
$\ip{w}{x}$, and transferring it to a classification loss requires a contraction step. Finally,
the factor $2$ in symmetrization comes from splitting a difference and is not shown optimal here.

\subsection{Future directions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{High probability bounds.} Adding McDiarmid's bounded differences inequality would
give the usual $\sup_f(\E f - \Ehat_S f)\le 2\Rad + 3B\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}$ with probability
$1-\delta$.
\item \textbf{Contraction (Talagrand's lemma).} $\Rad(\phi\circ\Fclass)\le L\,\Rad(\Fclass)$ for
$L$-Lipschitz $\phi$ would transfer the margin bound to the margin loss and yield the standard
margin bound for classification error.
\item \textbf{Sauer--Shelah and the growth function.} Establishing $\Pi_{\Fclass}(n)\le(en/d)^d$
for a class of VC dimension $d$ and combining it with Massart's lemma would give the VC bound
$\Rad\le\sqrt{2d\log(en/d)/n}$, making the comparison with the dimension-free margin bound
quantitative for a fixed structured class rather than through the shape of the bound.
\item \textbf{Lower bounds.} A matching lower bound for the Rademacher complexity of the ball and
of the cube --- both computed exactly here --- could be extended to a general Sudakov-type
minoration.
\item \textbf{From finite to general probability spaces.} Recasting the symmetrization argument in
terms of general product measures would remove the finiteness assumption, at the cost of
measurability side conditions for the supremum.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Closing remark}
The recurring theme is that capacity is a metric, not a combinatorial, notion. Counting how many
behaviours a class exhibits is legitimate and --- as the cube shows --- nearly optimal when the
class has no geometry to exploit. But when it does have geometry, as every norm-constrained
predictor class does, counting throws away exactly the information that matters and returns an
infinite answer to a question with a small finite one. Rademacher complexity is the measurement
that respects the geometry, and its operational meaning --- how well can this class fit noise? ---
is the same in both regimes.

  "demo": """"
Numerical demonstrations of generalization bounds via Rademacher complexity.

This script is fully self-contained: it uses only the Python standard library
(``math``, ``random``, ``itertools``) so that it runs anywhere without
installation.

The empirical Rademacher complexity of a set F of behaviour vectors in R^n is

    R(F) = (1 / 2^n) * sum over all sign patterns s in {-1,+1}^n of
                        sup_{v in F} (1/n) * <s, v>.

Every quantity below is computed either by exact enumeration of all 2^n sign
patterns (feasible for n <= 20) or by a closed-form formula, and the two are
compared against each other and against the theoretical bounds:

  1. A single hypothesis has complexity exactly 0.
  2. Monotonicity: F subset G  =>  R(F) <= R(G).
  3. The full sign cube {-1,+1}^n has complexity exactly 1, while Massart's
     finite class lemma predicts sqrt(2 log 2) = 1.1774...  -- tight to <18%.
  4. The Euclidean ball of radius r has complexity exactly r / sqrt(n),
     yet is an infinite class, so all counting bounds are vacuous for it.
  5. The margin bound: linear predictors with ||w|| <= W on data with
     ||x|| <= B have complexity at most W*B/sqrt(n).  The exact value is
     (W/n) * E_s ||sum_i s_i x_i||, which we compute by enumeration.
  6. The kernel margin bound depends on the kernel only through sup_x K(x,x);
     it is evaluated from the Gram matrix, never from the feature map.
  7. Dimension-dependent (VC-style) bounds c*sqrt(d/n) exceed the margin bound
     W*B/sqrt(n) as soon as d > (W*B/c)^2.
  8. Symmetrization: E_S sup_f (E f - Ehat_S f) <= 2 E_S R_S(F), verified by
     brute force on a small finite domain with an explicit product measure.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[List[float]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core machinery
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def sign_patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Yield all 2^n sign patterns in {-1,+1}^n."""
    for bits in itertools.product((1, -1), repeat=n):
        yield bits


def sign_average(sigma: Sequence[int], v: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The sign average A_sigma(v) = (1/n) sum_i sigma_i v_i."""
    n = len(v)
    return sum(s * x for s, x in zip(sigma, v)) / n


def rademacher_finite(vectors: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> float:
    """Exact empirical Rademacher complexity of a finite class of vectors.

    Enumerates all 2^n sign patterns; cost Theta(2^n * N * n).
    """
    n = len(vectors[0])
    total = 0.0
    for sigma in sign_patterns(n):
        total += max(sign_average(sigma, v) for v in vectors)
    return total / (2 ** n)


def rademacher_via_oracle(n: int, sup_oracle: Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], float]) -> float:
    """Exact complexity when the inner supremum is available in closed form."""
    total = 0.0
    for sigma in sign_patterns(n):
        total += sup_oracle(sigma)
    return total / (2 ** n)


def rademacher_monte_carlo(
    vectors: Sequence[Sequence[float]], draws: int, seed: int = 0
) -> float:
    """Monte Carlo estimate of the complexity of a finite class."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(vectors[0])
    total = 0.0
    for _ in range(draws):
        sigma = [rng.choice((1, -1)) for _ in range(n)]
        total += max(sign_average(sigma, v) for v in vectors)
    return total / draws


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theoretical bounds
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def massart_bound(num_vectors: int, radius: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Massart's finite class lemma:  r * sqrt(2 log N) / n."""
    if num_vectors <= 1:
        return 0.0
    return radius * math.sqrt(2.0 * math.log(num_vectors)) / n


def ball_complexity(radius: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Exact complexity of the Euclidean ball of radius r in R^n:  r / sqrt(n)."""
    return radius / math.sqrt(n)


def margin_bound(weight_norm: float, data_norm: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Margin bound for linear / kernel predictors:  W * B / sqrt(n)."""
    return weight_norm * data_norm / math.sqrt(n)


def vc_style_bound(constant: float, dimension: int, n: int) -> float:
    """A dimension-dependent bound of the classical shape  c * sqrt(d / n)."""
    return constant * math.sqrt(dimension / n)


def dimension_threshold(weight_norm: float, data_norm: float, constant: float) -> float:
    """The threshold (W*B/c)^2 beyond which c*sqrt(d/n) exceeds W*B/sqrt(n)."""
    return (weight_norm * data_norm / constant) ** 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Linear and kernel classes
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def euclidean_norm(v: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in v))


def exact_linear_complexity(points: Sequence[Sequence[float]], weight_norm: float) -> float:
    """Exact complexity of {x -> <w,x> : ||w|| <= W} on the given sample.

    For each sign pattern the inner supremum is (W/n)*||sum_i sigma_i x_i||,
    attained by w aligned with the signed sum.
    """
    n = len(points)
    dim = len(points[0])

    def sup_oracle(sigma: Tuple[int, ...]) -> float:
        signed = [sum(sigma[i] * points[i][k] for i in range(n)) for k in range(dim)]
        return weight_norm * euclidean_norm(signed) / n

    return rademacher_via_oracle(n, sup_oracle)


def gram_matrix(points: Sequence[Sequence[float]], kernel: Callable[[Sequence[float], Sequence[float]], float]) -> Matrix:
    n = len(points)
    return [[kernel(points[i], points[j]) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def exact_kernel_complexity(gram: Matrix, weight_norm: float) -> float:
    """Exact complexity of a kernel class, computed from the Gram matrix alone.

    Uses ||sum_i sigma_i phi(x_i)||^2 = sigma^T G sigma; the feature map is
    never required.
    """
    n = len(gram)

    def sup_oracle(sigma: Tuple[int, ...]) -> float:
        quad = 0.0
        for i in range(n):
            gi = gram[i]
            si = sigma[i]
            for j in range(n):
                quad += si * sigma[j] * gi[j]
        return weight_norm * math.sqrt(max(quad, 0.0)) / n

    return rademacher_via_oracle(n, sup_oracle)


def gaussian_kernel(gamma: float) -> Callable[[Sequence[float], Sequence[float]], float]:
    def k(a: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float]) -> float:
        d2 = sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b))
        return math.exp(-gamma * d2)
    return k


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Symmetrization on a small finite domain
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def brute_force_symmetrization(
    domain: Sequence[float],
    probs: Sequence[float],
    functions: Sequence[Callable[[float], float]],
    n: int,
) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Return (E_S gap(S), 2 * E_S Rhat_S(F)) by exhaustive enumeration.

    Cost Theta(|X|^n * (2^n + 1) * |F| * n); keep |X|, n small.
    """
    true_means = [sum(p * f(x) for p, x in zip(probs, domain)) for f in functions]

    expected_gap = 0.0
    expected_rad = 0.0
    for idx in itertools.product(range(len(domain)), repeat=n):
        weight = 1.0
        for i in idx:
            weight *= probs[i]

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Iterable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple

Vector = List[float]
Matrix = List[List[float]]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core machinery
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def sign_patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """Yield all 2^n sign patterns in {-1,+1}^n."""
    for bits in itertools.product((1, -1), repeat=n):
        yield bits


def sign_average(sigma: Sequence[int], v: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """The sign average A_sigma(v) = (1/n) sum_i sigma_i v_i."""
    n = len(v)
    return sum(s * x for s, x in zip(sigma, v)) / n


def rademacher_finite(vectors: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> float:
    """Exact empirical Rademacher complexity of a finite class of vectors.

    Enumerates all 2^n sign patterns; cost Theta(2^n * N * n).
    """
    n = len(vectors[0])
    total = 0.0
    for sigma in sign_patterns(n):
        total += max(sign_average(sigma, v) for v in vectors)
    return total / (2 ** n)


def rademacher_via_oracle(n: int, sup_oracle: Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], float]) -> float:
    """Exact complexity when the inner supremum is available in closed form."""
    total = 0.0
    for sigma in sign_patterns(n):
        total += sup_oracle(sigma)
    return total / (2 ** n)


def rademacher_monte_carlo(
    vectors: Sequence[Sequence[float]], draws: int, seed: int = 0
) -> float:
    """Monte Carlo estimate of the complexity of a finite class."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(vectors[0])
    total = 0.0
    for _ in range(draws):
        sigma = [rng.choice((1, -1)) for _ in range(n)]
        total += max(sign_average(sigma, v) for v in vectors)
    return total / draws


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Theoretical bounds
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def massart_bound(num_vectors: int, radius: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Massart's finite class lemma:  r * sqrt(2 log N) / n."""
    if num_vectors <= 1:
        return 0.0
    return radius * math.sqrt(2.0 * math.log(num_vectors)) / n


def ball_complexity(radius: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Exact complexity of the Euclidean ball of radius r in R^n:  r / sqrt(n)."""
    return radius / math.sqrt(n)


def margin_bound(weight_norm: float, data_norm: float, n: int) -> float:
    """Margin bound for linear / kernel predictors:  W * B / sqrt(n)."""
    return weight_norm * data_norm / math.sqrt(n)


def vc_style_bound(constant: float, dimension: int, n: int) -> float:
    """A dimension-dependent bound of the classical shape  c * sqrt(d / n)."""
    return constant * math.sqrt(dimension / n)


def dimension_threshold(weight_norm: float, data_norm: float, constant: float) -> float:
    """The threshold (W*B/c)^2 beyond which c*sqrt(d/n) exceeds W*B/sqrt(n)."""
    return (weight_norm * data_norm / constant) ** 2


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Linear and kernel classes
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def euclidean_norm(v: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in v))


def exact_linear_complexity(points: Sequence[Sequence[float]], weight_norm: float) -> float:
    """Exact complexity of {x -> <w,x> : ||w|| <= W} on the given sample.

    For each sign pattern the inner supremum is (W/n)*||sum_i sigma_i x_i||,
    attained by w aligned with the signed sum.
    """
    n = len(points)
    dim = len(points[0])

    def sup_oracle(sigma: Tuple[int, ...]) -> float:
        signed = [sum(sigma[i] * points[i][k] for i in range(n)) for k in range(dim)]
        return weight_norm * euclidean_norm(signed) / n

    return rademacher_via_oracle(n, sup_oracle)


def gram_matrix(points: Sequence[Sequence[float]], kernel: Callable[[Sequence[float], Sequence[float]], float]) -> Matrix:
    n = len(points)
    return [[kernel(points[i], points[j]) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]


def exact_kernel_complexity(gram: Matrix, weight_norm: float) -> float:
    """Exact complexity of a kernel class, computed from the Gram matrix alone.

    Uses ||sum_i sigma_i phi(x_i)||^2 = sigma^T G sigma; the feature map is
    never required.
    """
    n = len(gram)

    def sup_oracle(sigma: Tuple[int, ...]) -> float:
        quad = 0.0
        for i in range(n):
            gi = gram[i]
            si = sigma[i]
            for j in range(n):
                quad += si * sigma[j] * gi[j]
        return weight_norm * math.sqrt(max(quad, 0.0)) / n

    return rademacher_via_oracle(n, sup_oracle)


def gaussian_kernel(gamma: float) -> Callable[[Sequence[float], Sequence[float]], float]:
    def k(a: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float]) -> float:
        d2 = sum((x - y) ** 2 for x, y in zip(a, b))
        return math.exp(-gamma * d2)
    return k


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Symmetrization on a small finite domain
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def brute_force_symmetrization(
    domain: Sequence[float],
    probs: Sequence[float],
    functions: Sequence[Callable[[float], float]],
    n: int,
) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Return (E_S gap(S), 2 * E_S Rhat_S(F)) by exhaustive enumeration.

    Cost Theta(|X|^n * (2^n + 1) * |F| * n); keep |X|, n small.
    """
    true_means = [sum(p * f(x) for p, x in zip(probs, domain)) for f in functions]

    expected_gap = 0.0
    expected_rad = 0.0
    for idx in itertools.product(range(len(domain)), repeat=n):
        weight = 1.0
        for i in idx:
            weight *= probs[i]
        sample = [domain[i] for i in idx]

        gap = max(
            mu - sum(f(x) for x in sample) / n
            for mu, f in zip(true_means, functions)
        )
        expected_gap += weight * gap

        rad = 0.0
        for sigma in sign_patterns(n):
            rad += max(
                sum(s * f(x) for s, x in zip(sigma, sample)) / n
                for f in functions
            )
        rad /= 2 ** n
        expected_rad += weight * rad

    return expected_gap, 2.0 * expected_rad

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

Matrix = List[List[float]]
Vector = List[float]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Minimal dense linear algebra (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def solve(A: Matrix, b: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Solve the square system A x = b."""
    n = len(A)
    M = [row[:] + [b[i]] for i, row in enumerate(A)]
    for col in range(n):
        pivot = max(range(col, n), key=lambda r: abs(M[r][col]))
        if abs(M[pivot][col]) < 1e-14:
            raise ValueError("singular system")
        M[col], M[pivot] = M[pivot], M[col]
        p = M[col][col]
        for r in range(col + 1, n):
            factor = M[r][col] / p
            if factor == 0.0:
                continue
            for c in range(col, n + 1):
                M[r][c] -= factor * M[col][c]
    x = [0.0] * n
    for r in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        s = M[r][n] - sum(M[r][c] * x[c] for c in range(r + 1, n))
        x[r] = s / M[r][r]
    return x


def matmul_T(X: Matrix) -> Matrix:
    """Return X^T X."""
    n, d = len(X), len(X[0])
    out = [[0.0] * d for _ in range(d)]
    for i in range(n):
        row = X[i]
        for a in range(d):
            ra = row[a]
            if ra == 0.0:
                continue
            for b_ in range(d):
                out[a][b_] += ra * row[b_]
    return out


def matvec_T(X: Matrix, y: Vector) -> Vector:
    """Return X^T y."""
    n, d = len(X), len(X[0])
    out = [0.0] * d
    for i in range(n):
        yi = y[i]
        if yi == 0.0:
            continue
        row = X[i]
        for a in range(d):
            out[a] += row[a] * yi
    return out


def norm(v: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in v))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Ridge regression on random labels
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def ridge_weights(X: Matrix, y: Vector, lam: float) -> Vector:
    """(X^T X + lam I)^{-1} X^T y."""
    d = len(X[0])
    G = matmul_T(X)
    for a in range(d):
        G[a][a] += lam
    return solve(G, matvec_T(X, y))


def random_label_capacity(
    X: Matrix, lam: float, draws: int, seed: int = 0
) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Estimate the capacity by training on random labels.

    Returns (mean correlation with random labels, mean realized weight norm).
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    n = len(X)
    total_corr = 0.0
    total_norm = 0.0
    for _ in range(draws):
        sigma = [1.0 if rng.random() < 0.5 else -1.0 for _ in range(n)]
        w = ridge_weights(X, sigma, lam)
        preds = [sum(x * wi for x, wi in zip(row, w)) for row in X]
        total_corr += sum(s * p for s, p in zip(sigma, preds)) / n
        total_norm += norm(w)
    return total_corr / draws, total_norm / draws


def make_data(n: int, d: int, seed: int = 0) -> Matrix:
    """n points drawn uniformly from the unit sphere in R^d (so B = 1)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    X: Matrix = []
    for _ in range(n):
        raw = [rng.gauss(0.0, 1.0) for _ in range(d)]
        s = norm(raw)
        X.append([x / s for x in raw])
    return X

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Callable, Iterator, List, Sequence, Tuple


def sign_patterns(n: int) -> Iterator[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All 2^n elements of {-1,+1}^n, in Gray-free lexicographic order."""
    return itertools.product((1, -1), repeat=n)


def exact_rademacher(vectors: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> float:
    """Exact empirical Rademacher complexity of a finite class of behaviour vectors.

    R(F) = 2^{-n} * sum_sigma  max_{v in F} (1/n) <sigma, v>.

    Complexity: Theta(2^n * N * n) time, Theta(1) extra space.
    Exact to floating-point rounding; no randomness, no approximation.
    """
    if not vectors:
        raise ValueError("the class must be nonempty")
    n = len(vectors[0])
    if any(len(v) != n for v in vectors):
        raise ValueError("all behaviour vectors must have the same length")

    total = 0.0
    for sigma in sign_patterns(n):
        best = max(
            sum(s * x for s, x in zip(sigma, v)) / n
            for v in vectors
        )
        total += best
    return total / (2 ** n)


def exact_rademacher_from_oracle(n: int, sup_oracle: Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], float]) -> float:
    """Exact complexity when the inner supremum has a closed form.

    `sup_oracle(sigma)` must return  sup_{v in F} (1/n) <sigma, v>  for the given
    sign pattern.  This handles infinite classes (balls, norm-constrained linear
    and kernel classes) that cannot be enumerated.

    Complexity: Theta(2^n * cost(sup_oracle)).
    """
    total = 0.0
    for sigma in sign_patterns(n):
        total += sup_oracle(sigma)
    return total / (2 ** n)


def linear_class_oracle(
    points: Sequence[Sequence[float]], weight_norm: float
) -> Callable[[Tuple[int, ...]], float]:
    """Closed-form supremum for {x -> <w,x> : ||w|| <= W} on the given sample.

    The maximizing w is W times the unit vector along sum_i sigma_i x_i, so the
    supremum equals (W/n) * ||sum_i sigma_i x_i||.
    """
    n = len(points)
    dim = len(points[0])

    def oracle(sigma: Tuple[int, ...]) -> float:
        signed: List[float] = [
            sum(sigma[i] * points[i][k] for i in range(n)) for k in range(dim)
        ]
        return weight_norm * sum(c * c for c in signed) ** 0.5 / n

    return oracle

from __future__ import annotations

import math
import random
from typing import Callable, List, Sequence, Tuple


def monte_carlo_rademacher(
    n: int,
    sup_oracle: Callable[[Sequence[int]], float],
    draws: int,
    output_bound: float,
    confidence: float = 0.95,
    seed: int = 0,
) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Estimate  R = 2^{-n} sum_sigma sup_v (1/n)<sigma,v>  by sampling sign patterns.

    Returns (estimate, radius) where the true value lies within
    `estimate +/- radius` with probability at least `confidence`.

    Each term lies in [-output_bound, output_bound], so Hoeffding's inequality
    for an average of m independent bounded variables gives the radius
        output_bound * sqrt(2 * log(2/delta) / m),   delta = 1 - confidence.

    Complexity: Theta(m * cost(sup_oracle)); memory Theta(n).
    The estimator is unbiased and its error decays like 1/sqrt(m), independently
    of n, N and the dimension.
    """
    if draws <= 0:
        raise ValueError("draws must be positive")
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    total = 0.0
    for _ in range(draws):
        sigma: List[int] = [1 if rng.random() < 0.5 else -1 for _ in range(n)]
        total += sup_oracle(sigma)
    estimate = total / draws
    delta = 1.0 - confidence
    radius = output_bound * math.sqrt(2.0 * math.log(2.0 / delta) / draws)
    return estimate, radius


def finite_class_oracle(
    vectors: Sequence[Sequence[float]],
) -> Callable[[Sequence[int]], float]:
    """Inner supremum for a finite class: a maximum over the class."""
    n = len(vectors[0])

    def oracle(sigma: Sequence[int]) -> float:
        return max(sum(s * x for s, x in zip(sigma, v)) / n for v in vectors)

    return oracle


def kernel_class_oracle(
    gram: Sequence[Sequence[float]], weight_norm: float
) -> Callable[[Sequence[int]], float]:
    """Inner supremum for a kernel class, from the Gram matrix alone.

    sup_{||w||<=W} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i <w, phi(x_i)> = (W/n) * sqrt(sigma^T G sigma).
    The feature map is never needed -- this is what makes the bound usable in
    infinite-dimensional feature spaces.
    """
    n = len(gram)

    def oracle(sigma: Sequence[int]) -> float:
        quad = 0.0
        for i in range(n):
            row = gram[i]

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ClassProfile:
    """Everything the bounds need to know about a hypothesis class on a sample."""
    n: int                          # sample size
    output_bound: float             # B: uniform bound on |f(x)| over the class
    num_behaviours: Optional[int]   # N: number of distinct behaviours, or None if infinite
    euclidean_radius: Optional[float]   # r: bound on the length of behaviour vectors
    weight_norm: Optional[float] = None     # W, for linear / kernel classes
    data_norm: Optional[float] = None       # B_x = sup ||x|| or sqrt(sup K(x,x))
    dimension: Optional[int] = None         # d, for a dimension-dependent comparison
    vc_constant: float = 0.5                # c in the c*sqrt(d/n) shape


def applicable_bounds(p: ClassProfile) -> List[Tuple[str, float]]:
    """All capacity bounds that apply, as (name, value) pairs.

    * trivial output bound:      B
    * Massart counting bound:    r * sqrt(2 log N) / n           (needs N finite)
    * Euclidean ball bound:      r / sqrt(n)                     (needs r)
    * margin / kernel bound:     W * B_x / sqrt(n)               (linear / kernel)

    A dimension-dependent bound c*sqrt(d/n) is reported for comparison only; it is
    not a bound proved here but the shape any VC-derived argument produces.

    Complexity: O(1).
    """
    out: List[Tuple[str, float]] = [("trivial output bound  B", p.output_bound)]
    if p.num_behaviours is not None and p.num_behaviours >= 1 and p.euclidean_radius is not None:
        if p.num_behaviours == 1:
            out.append(("Massart  r*sqrt(2 log N)/n", 0.0))
        else:
            out.append((
                "Massart  r*sqrt(2 log N)/n",
                p.euclidean_radius * math.sqrt(2.0 * math.log(p.num_behaviours)) / p.n,
            ))
    if p.euclidean_radius is not None:
        out.append(("ball  r/sqrt(n)", p.euclidean_radius / math.sqrt(p.n)))
    if p.weight_norm is not None and p.data_norm is not None:
        out.append(("margin/kernel  W*B/sqrt(n)",
                    p.weight_norm * p.data_norm / math.sqrt(p.n)))
    return out


def certified_capacity(p: ClassProfile) -> Tuple[str, float]:
    """The tightest applicable capacity bound and the name of the bound achieving it."""
    bounds = applicable_bounds(p)
    name, value = min(bounds, key=lambda kv: kv[1])
    return name, value


def generalization_guarantee(p: ClassProfile) -> Tuple[str, float]:
    """Expected uniform deviation bound: twice the certified capacity.

    By symmetrization,  E_S sup_f (E f - Ehat_S f)  <=  2 * E_S Rhat_S(F),
    so any uniform-in-sample capacity bound doubles into a generalization bound.
    """
    name, value = certified_capacity(p)
    return name, 2.0 * value


def dimension_comparison(p: ClassProfile) -> Optional[Tuple[float, float, bool]]:
    """Return (vc_style_value, crossover_dimension, margin_is_better) or None.

    The crossover is at d = (W*B/c)^2: beyond it the dimension-dependent bound is
    strictly larger, hence strictly weaker, than the dimension-free margin bound.
    """
    if p.dimension is None or p.weight_norm is None or p.data_norm is None:
        return None
    vc = p.vc_constant * math.sqrt(p.dimension / p.n)
    crossover = (p.weight_norm * p.data_norm / p.vc_constant) ** 2
    margin = p.weight_norm * p.data_norm / math.sqrt(p.n)
    return vc, crossover, margin < vc

    print("kernel class :", certified_capacity(kernel))
    print("  guarantee  :", generalization_guarantee(kernel))
    print("  vs dimension:", dimension_comparison(kernel))

    x = RNG.standard_normal((n, d))
    x /= np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1, keepdims=True)

      <p class="note">

        it points along <code>∑<sub>i</sub>σ<sub>i</sub>x<sub>i</sub></code>, and the
        correlation it achieves is <code>(W/n)‖∑<sub>i</sub>σ<sub>i</sub>x<sub>i</sub>‖</code>
        — exactly the inner supremum. The complexity is the average of that green number over all

        (3) Cluster all the points together with the mouse: the signed sums stop cancelling, the
        exact value climbs toward the bound. (4) Spread them out symmetrically: cancellation is

<script>
(function(){
  const cv = document.getElementById('cv'), ctx = cv.getContext('2d');
  const nS=document.getElementById('n'), WS=document.getElementById('W'), BS=document.getElementById('B');
  let n = +nS.value, W = +WS.value, Bscale = +BS.value;
  let pts = [];              // unit-scale points in [-1,1]^2
  let sigma = [];
  let animating = false;

  function randomSample(k){
    const a=[];
    for(let i=0;i<k;i++){
      const t = Math.random()*2*Math.PI, r = Math.sqrt(Math.random());
      a.push([r*Math.cos(t), r*Math.sin(t)]);
    }
    return a;
  }
  function ringSample(k){
    const a=[];
    for(let i=0;i<k;i++){ const t = 2*Math.PI*i/k; a.push([Math.cos(t), Math.sin(t)]); }
    return a;
  }
  function resize(k){
    if(pts.length < k) pts = pts.concat(randomSample(k - pts.length));
    else pts = pts.slice(0,k);
    newFlips();
  }
  function newFlips(){ sigma = pts.map(()=> Math.random()<0.5 ? 1 : -1); }

  function signedSum(sg){
    let sx=0, sy=0;
    for(let i=0;i<pts.length;i++){ sx += sg[i]*pts[i][0]*Bscale; sy += sg[i]*pts[i][1]*Bscale; }
    return [sx,sy];
  }
  function corr(sg){
    const [sx,sy] = signedSum(sg);
    return W*Math.hypot(sx,sy)/pts.length;
  }
  // exact complexity: enumerate all 2^n sign patterns
  function exactComplexity(){
    const k = pts.length, total = 1<<k;
    let acc = 0;
    for(let m=0;m<total;m++){
      let sx=0, sy=0;
      for(let i=0;i<k;i++){
        const s = (m>>i & 1) ? 1 : -1;
        sx += s*pts[i][0]*Bscale; sy += s*pts[i][1]*Bscale;
      }
      acc += Math.hypot(sx,sy);
    }
    return W*acc/(total*k);
  }
  // largest data norm actually present
  function dataRadius(){
    let b=0; for(const p of pts) b=Math.max(b, Math.hypot(p[0],p[1])*Bscale); return b;
  }

  // ---------- drawing ----------
  const PAD=42;
  function toPix(p){
    const w=cv.width, h=cv.height, R=Math.min(w,h)/2-PAD;
    return [w/2 + p[0]*Bscale*R/2, h/2 - p[1]*Bscale*R/2];
  }
  function draw(){
    const w=cv.width, h=cv.height;
    ctx.clearRect(0,0,w,h);
    // grid
    ctx.strokeStyle='#1b2438'; ctx.lineWidth=1;
    for(let g=-2;g<=2;g+=0.5){
      const [x0,y0]=toPix([g,-2.4]), [x1,y1]=toPix([g,2.4]);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x0,y0); ctx.lineTo(x1,y1); ctx.stroke();
      const [a0,b0]=toPix([-2.4,g]), [a1,b1]=toPix([2.4,g]);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(a0,b0); ctx.lineTo(a1,b1); ctx.stroke();
    }
    // axes
    ctx.strokeStyle='#2c3a58'; ctx.lineWidth=1.4;
    const [ax0,ay0]=toPix([-2.4,0]), [ax1,ay1]=toPix([2.4,0]);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(ax0,ay0); ctx.lineTo(ax1,ay1); ctx.stroke();
    const [bx0,by0]=toPix([0,-2.4]), [bx1,by1]=toPix([0,2.4]);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(bx0,by0); ctx.lineTo(bx1,by1); ctx.stroke();

    // best weight direction (green arrow), scaled for visibility
    const [sx,sy] = signedSum(sigma);
    const nrm = Math.hypot(sx,sy);
    if(nrm > 1e-9){
      const ux = sx/nrm, uy = sy/nrm;
      const [ox,oy] = toPix([0,0]);
      const [tx,ty] = toPix([ux*1.55/Bscale, uy*1.55/Bscale]);

      ctx.strokeStyle='rgba(74,217,164,.28)'; ctx.lineWidth=2; ctx.setLineDash([7,6]);
      const [p0x,p0y]=toPix([-uy*2.4/Bscale, ux*2.4/Bscale]);
      const [p1x,p1y]=toPix([ uy*2.4/Bscale,-ux*2.4/Bscale]);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(p0x,p0y); ctx.lineTo(p1x,p1y); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.setLineDash([]);
      ctx.strokeStyle='#4ad9a4'; ctx.lineWidth=3;
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(ox,oy); ctx.lineTo(tx,ty); ctx.stroke();
      const ang=Math.atan2(ty-oy,tx-ox);
      ctx.fillStyle='#4ad9a4';
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.moveTo(tx,ty);
      ctx.lineTo(tx-12*Math.cos(ang-0.4), ty-12*Math.sin(ang-0.4));
      ctx.lineTo(tx-12*Math.cos(ang+0.4), ty-12*Math.sin(ang+0.4));
      ctx.closePath(); ctx.fill();
      ctx.fillStyle='#4ad9a4'; ctx.font='13px ui-monospace,monospace';
      ctx.fillText('best w  (norm W)', tx+8, ty-8);
    }

    // points
    for(let i=0;i<pts.length;i++){
      const [x,y]=toPix(pts[i]);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(x,y,9,0,2*Math.PI);
      ctx.fillStyle = sigma[i]>0 ? '#4aa3ff' : '#ffb35c';
      ctx.fill();
      ctx.strokeStyle='#0b101a'; ctx.lineWidth=2; ctx.stroke();
      ctx.fillStyle='#06101f'; ctx.font='bold 11px ui-monospace,monospace';
      ctx.textAlign='center'; ctx.textBaseline='middle';
      ctx.fillText(sigma[i]>0?'+':'−', x, y+0.5);
      ctx.textAlign='start'; ctx.textBaseline='alphabetic';
    }
    ctx.fillStyle='#93a2bd'; ctx.font='12px ui-monospace,monospace';
    ctx.fillText('random labels: blue = +1, orange = −1  •  drag points', 12, h-12);
  }

  function fmt(x){ return x.toFixed(5); }
  function update(){
    n = +nS.value; W = +WS.value; Bscale = +BS.value;
    document.getElementById('nv').textContent = n;
    document.getElementById('Wv').textContent = W.toFixed(2);
    document.getElementById('Bv').textContent = Bscale.toFixed(2);
    if(pts.length !== n) resize(n);

    const B = dataRadius();
    const ex = exactComplexity();
    const mg = W*B/Math.sqrt(n);
    const bl = W*B;                         // r/sqrt(n) with r = W B sqrt(n)
    const tv = W*B;                         // trivial output bound
    const cu = corr(sigma);

    document.getElementById('exact').textContent = fmt(ex);
    document.getElementById('margin').textContent = fmt(mg);
    document.getElementById('ball').textContent = fmt(bl);
    document.getElementById('triv').textContent = fmt(tv);
    document.getElementById('cur').textContent = fmt(cu);

    const scale = Math.max(tv, 1e-9);
    document.getElementById('barExact').style.width = (100*ex/scale)+'%';
    document.getElementById('barMargin').style.width = (100*mg/scale)+'%';
    document.getElementById('barBall').style.width = (100*bl/scale)+'%';
    document.getElementById('barTriv').style.width = '100%';

    const ratio = mg>0 ? ex/mg : 0;
    const v = document.getElementById('verdict');
    if(ratio > 0.93){
      v.className='verdict warn';
      v.innerHTML = '<b>Cancellation is weak here.</b> The exact complexity is '+
        (100*ratio).toFixed(1)+'% of the margin bound — the sample is nearly aligned, so the '+
        'signed sums <code>∑σ<sub>i</sub>x<sub>i</sub></code> do not cancel and '+
        'Cauchy–Schwarz is almost an equality. This is the worst case the bound protects against.';
    } else {
      v.className='verdict';
      v.innerHTML = '<b>Cancellation is doing work.</b> The exact complexity is only '+
        (100*ratio).toFixed(1)+'% of the margin bound <code>WB/√n</code>. The identity '+
        '<code>E[σ<sub>i</sub>σ<sub>j</sub>] = 0</code> for <code>i≠j</code> means '+
        'signed sums of a spread-out sample are much shorter than the worst case — which is '+
        'precisely the extra factor <code>1/√n</code> the margin bound buys over the crude '+
        'ball bound <code>WB</code>.';
    }
    draw();
  }

  // ---------- interaction ----------
  let dragIdx=-1;
  function mouseToUnit(e){
    const r=cv.getBoundingClientRect();
    const x=(e.clientX-r.left)*cv.width/r.width, y=(e.clientY-r.top)*cv.height/r.height;
    const R=Math.min(cv.width,cv.height)/2-PAD;
    return [ (x-cv.width/2)*2/(R*Bscale), (cv.height/2-y)*2/(R*Bscale) ];
  }
  cv.addEventListener('mousedown', e=>{
    const u=mouseToUnit(e);
    let best=-1, bd=1e9;
    for(let i=0;i<pts.length;i++){
      const d=Math.hypot(pts[i][0]-u[0], pts[i][1]-u[1]);
      if(d<bd){bd=d;best=i;}
    }
    if(bd < 0.16) dragIdx=best;
  });
  window.addEventListener('mousemove', e=>{
    if(dragIdx<0) return;
    const u=mouseToUnit(e);
    pts[dragIdx]=[Math.max(-2,Math.min(2,u[0])), Math.max(-2,Math.min(2,u[1]))];
    update();
  });
  window.addEventListener('mouseup', ()=>{ dragIdx=-1; });

  document.getElementById('flip').onclick = ()=>{ newFlips(); update(); };
  document.getElementById('rand').onclick = ()=>{ pts=randomSample(+nS.value); newFlips(); update(); };
  document.getElementById('ring').onclick = ()=>{ pts=ringSample(+nS.value); newFlips(); update(); };
  document.getElementById('play').onclick = function(){
    animating=!animating; this.textContent = animating ? '⏸ Pause' : '▶ Animate';
    (function loop(){ if(!animating) return; newFlips(); update(); setTimeout(loop, 420); })();
  };
  [nS,WS,BS].forEach(s=> s.addEventListener('input', update));

  pts = randomSample(n); newFlips(); update();
})();
</script>

      "html": "<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">

<style>

<body>
<div class="wrap">
  <h1>Counting versus Geometry: The Bound Explorer</h1>
  <p class="sub">
    Four different ways to bound the capacity of a hypothesis class, plotted together.
    <b>Counting bounds</b> control the class through the number <code>N</code> of behaviours it
    realizes on the sample; <b>geometric bounds</b> control it through the size of the weight
    budget <code>W</code> and the data <code>B</code>. Move the sliders to see which one wins
    where — and watch the counting bounds fall off a cliff when the class becomes infinite.
  </p>

  <div class="grid">
    <div class="panel">
      <div class="tabs">
        <button class="on" data-mode="n">capacity vs. sample size n</button>
        <button data-mode="d">capacity vs. dimension d</button>
        <button data-mode="N">capacity vs. class size N</button>
      </div>
      <canvas id="cv" width="740" height="470"></canvas>
      <p class="note">
        <b>Massart's finite class lemma</b> gives <code>B√(2 log N / n)</code> for a class of
        <code>N</code> behaviours bounded by <code>B</code>. The <b>margin bound</b> gives
        <code>WB/√n</code> for linear or kernel predictors of weight-norm at most
        <code>W</code> — with no reference to dimension at all. A <b>VC-style bound</b> has the
        shape <code>c√(d/n)</code>. The <b>exact value for the Euclidean ball</b> of radius
        <code>r</code> is <code>r/√n</code> — an infinite class, so counting says nothing
        about it whatsoever.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="panel">
      <h2>Parameters</h2>
      <div class="ctrl"><label>sample size n <b><span id="nv">200</span></b></label>
        <input id="n" type="range" min="10" max="5000" step="10" value="200"></div>
      <div class="ctrl"><label>weight budget W <b><span id="Wv">1.50</span></b></label>

      <div class="ctrl"><label>data bound B <b><span id="Bv">1.00</span></b></label>
        <input id="B" type="range" min="0.1" max="3" step="0.05" value="1"></div>
      <div class="ctrl"><label>class size log₁₀N <b><span id="Nv">3.0</span></b></label>
        <input id="N" type="range" min="0.3" max="12" step="0.1" value="3"></div>
      <div class="ctrl"><label>dimension d <b><span id="dv">400</span></b></label>
        <input id="d" type="range" min="1" max="5000" step="1" value="400"></div>
      <div class="ctrl"><label>VC constant c <b><span id="cv2">0.50</span></b></label>
        <input id="c" type="range" min="0.05" max="3" step="0.05" value="0.5"></div>

      <h2 style="margin-top:20px">At the current settings</h2>
      <table>
        <tr><th>bound</th><th>value</th></tr>
        <tr><td><span class="swatch" style="background:var(--blue)"></span>margin / kernel  WB/√n</td><td class="num" id="rM">–</td></tr>
        <tr><td><span class="swatch" style="background:var(--orange)"></span>Massart  B√(2 log N/n)</td><td class="num" id="rA">–</td></tr>
        <tr><td><span class="swatch" style="background:var(--red)"></span>VC-style  c√(d/n)</td><td class="num" id="rV">–</td></tr>
        <tr><td><span class="swatch" style="background:var(--green)"></span>ball, exact  r/√n (r = B√n)</td><td class="num" id="rB">–</td></tr>
      </table>
      <div class="verdict" id="verdict"></div>

        The dimension crossover is at <code>d = (WB/c)²</code>: for every larger dimension the
        dimension-dependent bound is strictly worse, and the ratio grows like <code>√d</code>.
        Push <code>d</code> to the right-hand end of its range and compare the red and blue numbers.
      </p>

<script>
(function(){
  const cv=document.getElementById('cv'), ctx=cv.getContext('2d');
  const ids=['n','W','B','N','d','c'];
  const el={}; ids.forEach(i=> el[i]=document.getElementById(i));
  let mode='n';

  function P(){
    return { n:+el.n.value, W:+el.W.value, B:+el.B.value,
             N:Math.pow(10,+el.N.value), d:+el.d.value, c:+el.c.value };
  }
  const margin  = (p,n)=> p.W*p.B/Math.sqrt(n);
  const massart = (p,n,N)=> p.B*Math.sqrt(2*Math.log(Math.max(N,1.0001))/n);
  const vcb     = (p,n,d)=> p.c*Math.sqrt(d/n);
  const ballv   = (p,n)=> p.B;   // r/sqrt(n) with r = B sqrt(n)

  const PADL=68, PADR=22, PADT=26, PADB=52;
  function axes(xmin,xmax,ymin,ymax,xlabel,ylabel,logx){
    const w=cv.width,h=cv.height;
    ctx.clearRect(0,0,w,h);
    ctx.strokeStyle='#1b2438'; ctx.lineWidth=1;
    ctx.fillStyle='#6f80a0'; ctx.font='11px ui-monospace,monospace';
    // y grid (log)
    const decades=[];
    for(let e=Math.floor(Math.log10(ymin)); e<=Math.ceil(Math.log10(ymax)); e++) decades.push(e);
    decades.forEach(e=>{
      const v=Math.pow(10,e); if(v<ymin||v>ymax) return;
      const y=Y(v,ymin,ymax);
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(PADL,y); ctx.lineTo(w-PADR,y); ctx.stroke();
      ctx.textAlign='right'; ctx.fillText(v>=1? v.toString() : v.toExponential(0), PADL-8, y+4);
    });
    // x grid
    const ticks=6;
    for(let i=0;i<=ticks;i++){
      const t=i/ticks;
      const xv = logx ? Math.pow(10, Math.log10(xmin)+t*(Math.log10(xmax)-Math.log10(xmin)))
                      : xmin + t*(xmax-xmin);
      const x=X(xv,xmin,xmax,logx);

### A guided tour of Rademacher complexity, generalization, and why counting hypotheses is the wrong idea

---

## 0. The one-sentence version

> **A model class is safe exactly to the extent that it *cannot* fit random labels.**

Everything on this page is an elaboration of that sentence: how to turn it into a number, how to
compute that number exactly for the classes that matter, and why it beats the classical
"count the hypotheses" approach so decisively that the classical approach sometimes says nothing
at all.

No background beyond linear algebra and the phrase "expected value" is assumed. Dense material is
tucked behind expandable panels — open them if you want the full argument, skip them if you want
the story.

---

## 1. The experiment that defines everything

Take your training set of $n$ examples. **Throw away the labels.** Replace them with independent
coin flips $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n \in \{-1,+1\}$. Now ask your model class to fit *those*.

If it can, your model is a memorizer. If it can't, and it still fits the real data, that fit means
something.

The **empirical Rademacher complexity** turns this into a number. Write $F \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
for the class as seen through the sample — each hypothesis $f$ contributes its vector of outputs
$(f(x_1),\dots,f(x_n))$. Then

$$\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(F) \;=\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}}_{\text{over all } 2^n \text{ coin-flip patterns}}\ \Big[\ \underbrace{\sup_{v\in F}}_{\text{the best the class can do}}\ \underbrace{\tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_i \sigma_i v_i}_{\text{correlation with the noise}}\ \Big].$$

Play with the definition directly. Below, the class is "all linear predictors with weight norm at
most $W$", the sample points are draggable, and the exact value — computed by enumerating *every
single one* of the $2^n$ sign patterns, no sampling — is shown next to the theoretical bounds.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

**Things worth discovering in the widget:**

- Slide $n$ upward. Capacity falls like $1/\sqrt n$. More data, less room to chase noise.
- Slide $W$ upward. Capacity grows *linearly*. This is what regularization buys you, quantitatively.
- Drag all the points into a tight cluster. The signed sums stop cancelling and the exact value
  climbs to meet the bound. Spread them out symmetrically and it plunges. **Cancellation is the
  mechanism.**

<details>
<summary><b>The four elementary facts that set the scale</b> (click to expand)</summary>

These follow from one observation: the map $\sigma \mapsto -\sigma$ shuffles the $2^n$ sign
patterns among themselves.

1. **A single hypothesis has complexity exactly $0$.** With $F=\{v\}$ there is no supremum to
   exploit, and averaging $\frac1n\sum_i \sigma_i v_i$ over all patterns gives zero because each
   coordinate is $+1$ as often as $-1$. *A class with no choices cannot overfit.*
2. **Monotonicity.** $F \subseteq G \Rightarrow \widehat{\mathcal{R}}(F) \le \widehat{\mathcal{R}}(G)$.
   A bigger menu correlates at least as well.
3. **Nonnegativity.** For nonempty $F$, $\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(F)\ge0$. Fix any $v\in F$: at $\sigma$
   the supremum is at least $\frac1n\langle\sigma,v\rangle$, at $-\sigma$ it is at least
   $-\frac1n\langle\sigma,v\rangle$, and the two lower bounds sum to zero.
4. **Uniform bound.** If $|v_i|\le B$ for all $v\in F$ and all $i$, then
   $\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(F)\le B$. You cannot correlate harder than your outputs allow.

So capacity lives in $[0, B]$, and the whole game is finding where in that interval a class sits.

</details>

---

## 2. Why the number matters: symmetrization

The definition would be a curiosity if it didn't *control* something. It does, and this is the
load-bearing theorem of the subject.

> **Symmetrization Theorem.** Let $\mathrm{gap}(S) = \sup_{f}\big(\mathbb{E}f - \widehat{\mathbb{E}}_S f\big)$
> be the worst overestimate of quality that the sample $S$ can produce, over the whole class. Then
> $$\mathbb{E}_S\big[\mathrm{gap}(S)\big] \;\le\; 2\,\mathbb{E}_S\big[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_S(\mathcal{F})\big].$$

In words: **the expected amount by which a finite sample can fool you is at most twice the
expected ability of your class to fit noise.**

<details>
<summary><b>The proof — two beautiful moves</b> (click to reveal)</summary>

**Move 1: the ghost sample.** The true mean $\mathbb{E}f$ is unknown, so replace it by the
empirical mean on a second, imaginary sample $S'$ drawn independently from the same distribution.
Since $\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{S'}f$ is unbiased for $\mathbb{E}f$, and since the supremum of an
average is at most the average of the suprema (Jensen's inequality applied to $\max$),

$$\mathbb{E}_S[\mathrm{gap}(S)] \;\le\; \mathbb{E}_{S,S'}\Big[\sup_f \tfrac1n\textstyle\sum_i\big(f(x_i') - f(x_i)\big)\Big].$$

**Move 2: the swap.** Because $x_i$ and $x_i'$ are i.i.d., exchanging them changes nothing about
the joint distribution. Exchanging the $i$-th pair is *the same operation* as flipping the sign of
the $i$-th difference $f(x_i')-f(x_i)$. So for **every** sign pattern $\sigma$ we may insert
$\sigma_i$ in front of the $i$-th difference for free. Average over all $2^n$ patterns, split the
difference with $\max(a+b)\le\max a + \max b$, and each half is exactly an empirical Rademacher
complexity. Total: $2\,\mathbb{E}_S[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_S]$. $\blacksquare$

The factor $2$ is the price of the split; the rate is untouched.

</details>

The consequence is the whole reason to care: **any bound on noise-fitting is a generalization
guarantee.** So: how do we bound noise-fitting?

---

## 3. Route one — counting. It's better than you'd think.

The oldest instinct is to count. If the class produces only $N$ distinct behaviours on the sample,
the supremum is a maximum over $N$ things, and a maximum of $N$ sub-Gaussian quantities is not
much bigger than $\sqrt{2\log N}$ times their scale.

> **Massart's Finite Class Lemma.** If $F$ consists of $N$ vectors, each of Euclidean length at
> most $r$, then
> $$\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(F) \;\le\; \frac{r\sqrt{2\log N}}{n}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>The Chernoff argument in four steps</b> (click to reveal)</summary>

Fix $\lambda > 0$ and write $M(\sigma) = \max_{v}\sum_i \sigma_i v_i$.

1. **Jensen.** $\exp\big(\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_\sigma M(\sigma)\big) \le \mathbb{E}_\sigma e^{\lambda M(\sigma)}$.
2. **Max $\le$ sum.** $e^{\lambda M(\sigma)} = \max_v e^{\lambda\langle\sigma,v\rangle} \le \sum_{v\in F} e^{\lambda\langle\sigma,v\rangle}$ — this is where the factor $N$ enters.
3. **Exact MGF.** Independence across coordinates factorizes the moment generating function:
   $$\mathbb{E}_\sigma \exp\Big(\lambda\sum_i \sigma_i v_i\Big) = \prod_i \cosh(\lambda v_i) \le \prod_i e^{\lambda^2 v_i^2/2} \le e^{\lambda^2 r^2/2},$$
   using $\cosh t \le e^{t^2/2}$ (compare Taylor coefficients: $\tfrac{1}{(2k)!}\le\tfrac{1}{2^kk!}$).
4. **Optimize.** Taking logs leaves $\frac{\log N}{\lambda} + \frac{\lambda r^2}{2}$; the balancing
   choice $\lambda = \sqrt{2\log N}/r$ yields $r\sqrt{2\log N}$. Divide by $n$.

</details>

### How good is it? Exactly this good.

Take the **hardest class imaginable**: the full sign cube $\{-1,+1\}^n$, every possible labelling
of the sample. Every $\sigma$ finds its perfect match $v = \sigma$, so
$\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(\{-1,+1\}^n) = 1$ **exactly**. And Massart, with $N=2^n$ and $r=\sqrt n$,
predicts

$$\frac{\sqrt n\,\sqrt{2\log 2^n}}{n} \;=\; \sqrt{2\log 2} \;\approx\; 1.1774,$$

for *every* $n$ — the $n$'s cancel completely. One can pin the constant precisely:
$1 \le \sqrt{2\log2} < \tfrac65$. **Counting overestimates the truth by under 18%, forever.**

So counting is not a crude tool. On unstructured classes it is essentially the right answer.

{{algorithm:0}}

Run the enumeration above on the cube for $n=1,\dots,10$ and you will get $1.000000000000$ every
time — no sampling, no approximation, just the definition.

## 4. Route two — geometry. And the moment counting dies.

Now the twist. Consider the **Euclidean ball** $\mathrm{Ball}_n(r) = \{v : \sum_i v_i^2 \le r^2\}$:
all behaviour vectors of length at most $r$. Two facts about it stand in flat opposition.

**Fact A — its complexity is exactly $r/\sqrt n$.** Not "at most". Exactly.

<details>
<summary><b>Both directions in three lines</b> (click to reveal)</summary>

*Upper:* Cauchy–Schwarz, $\frac1n\sum_i\sigma_i v_i \le \frac1n\|\sigma\|\|v\| \le \frac{\sqrt n\,r}{n} = \frac{r}{\sqrt n}$.

*Lower:* the vector $v^\sigma = \frac{r}{\sqrt n}\sigma$ lies **in** the ball (length exactly $r$)
and achieves $\frac1n\sum_i\sigma_i\cdot\frac{r}{\sqrt n}\sigma_i = \frac{r}{\sqrt n}$.

Since the supremum equals $r/\sqrt n$ for *every* sign pattern, the average is $r/\sqrt n$ too.
$\blacksquare$

</details>

**Fact B — the ball is an infinite class.** It contains the whole segment
$\{(t,0,\dots,0) : 0 \le t \le r\}$. So $N = \infty$, and *every* counting bound — Massart, growth
functions, [Sauer–Shelah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sauer%E2%80%93Shelah_lemma), the standard
[VC route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapnik%E2%80%93Chervonenkis_dimension) — reads
"$\widehat{\mathcal{R}} \le \infty$". True. Useless.

Here is a class whose capacity is a small, *exactly computable* number, and about which counting
says literally nothing.

The picture below makes the exactness visible: for $n=2$ the maximizers sit on the boundary of the
circle, and the level sets of the correlation are tangent there. That tangency *is* Cauchy–Schwarz.
